title: Statistical Reasoning: Missing Values, Means & Sampling
description: Explore essential mathematical concepts through carefully crafted questions. Strengthen your understanding, practice your reasoning, and learn at your own pace.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate which sampling approach is likely to produce a more reliable estimate of a population parameter.
questions.question: A polling company wants to estimate the opinion of a city with 2 million residents. Which approach would most likely produce the most reliable estimate?

options.label: A
options.text: Asking 20 residents who live on the same street

options.label: B
options.text: Asking every resident who happens to visit the mayor's office in one day

options.label: C
options.text: Randomly sampling 2,000 residents from across the whole city

questions.explanation: A larger, randomly selected sample drawn from across the entire population reduces both sampling error and bias, making the estimate more reliable. Small or non-random samples (like one street, or people who choose to visit an office) are more likely to be unrepresentative of the whole population.
questions.hint: Consider both the sample size and whether the sample was chosen randomly from the whole population.

questions.learningObjective: Find a missing value in a data set given the mean and the other observations.
questions.question: A data set of \(4\) running times (minutes) has a mean of \(42.2\). If \(3\) of the values are \(12, 60, 55\), what is the missing value?
questions.explanation: The total of all four values is \(4(42.2)=168.8\). The known values sum to \(12+60+55=127\), so the missing value is \(168.8-127=41.8\).
questions.hint: Multiply the mean by the number of values to find the total sum, then subtract the known values.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish between a population and a sample in a real-world data collection scenario.
questions.question: A quality inspector tests 50 phones randomly selected from today's production of 5,000 phones. Does this describe a population or a sample?

options.label: A
options.text: sample

options.label: B
options.text: population

options.label: C
options.text: neither a population nor a sample

questions.explanation: Because only a subset of the full group is measured, this data set represents a sample drawn from a larger population.
questions.hint: A population includes every member of the group; a sample includes only part of it.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an example of continuous numerical data.
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of continuous data?

options.label: A
options.text: The exact weight of a bag of rice in kilograms

options.label: B
options.text: The number of bags of rice sold in a store

options.label: C
options.text: The number of customers who bought rice

questions.explanation: Continuous data can take any value within a range, including decimals, such as weight. Counts of bags or customers are discrete because they can only take whole-number values.
questions.hint: Continuous data can be measured to any level of precision; discrete data can only be counted in whole units.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a data set.
questions.question: A set of weekly sales ($) was recorded as \(17, 84, 30, 51, 17, 28\). What is the mean of this data set?
questions.explanation: Sum all the values: \(17 + 84 + 30 + 51 + 17 + 28 = 227\). Divide by the number of values, \(n=6\): \(\bar{x} = \frac{227}{6} = 37.83\).
questions.hint: Add all the values together, then divide by how many values there are: \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}\).

questions.learningObjective: Find a missing value in a data set given the mean and the other observations.
questions.question: A data set of \(4\) daily temperatures, measured in degrees Celsius, has a mean of \(35.2\). If \(3\) of the values are \(22,56,26\), what is the missing value?
questions.explanation: The total of all four values is \(4(35.2)=140.8\). The known values sum to \(22+56+26=104\), so the missing value is \(140.8-104=36.8\).
questions.hint: Multiply the mean by the number of values to find the total sum, then subtract the known values.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize how a truncated axis can create a misleading visual impression of a data comparison.
questions.question: A bar chart comparing two companies' annual revenue has its vertical axis starting at \(90\) instead of \(0\). Company X's bar looks twice as tall as Company Y's, even though Company X's revenue is only slightly higher. What statistical issue does this illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: The data itself must have been recorded incorrectly

options.label: B
options.text: A truncated (non-zero) axis can visually exaggerate small differences between values

options.label: C
options.text: Bar charts can never be used to compare two companies fairly

questions.explanation: Starting a bar chart's axis at a value other than zero distorts the visual proportions between bars, making a small actual difference appear much larger than it really is. This is a common way graphs can mislead viewers, even when the underlying numbers are accurate.
questions.hint: Think about how the starting point of the vertical axis affects the apparent height of the bars.

questions.learningObjective: Find a missing value in a data set given the mean and the other observations.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a claim about a data set is mathematically consistent with a given mean.
questions.question: A data set has \(n=5\) values with a mean of \(25\). A student claims that all 5 values in the data set are greater than \(30\). Is this possible?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, this is always possible regardless of the mean

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the sum of the values would then exceed the total implied by the mean

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, as long as the median is also greater than the mean

questions.explanation: If the mean is \(25\) for \(n=5\) values, the total sum must be \(25 \times 5 = 125\). If every value were greater than \(30\), the sum would have to exceed \(150\), which is greater than \(125\). This is a contradiction, so it is impossible for all values to exceed the mean by that much.
questions.hint: Check whether the claim is consistent with the total sum implied by the mean: \(\text{sum} = \bar{x} \times n\).

questions.learningObjective: Select the most appropriate measure of central tendency for a given data scenario.
questions.question: A data set of household incomes contains one extremely high value (an outlier). Which measure of central tendency best represents the typical household in this case?

options.label: B

questions.learningObjective: Interpret standard deviation as a measure of the spread of a data set.
questions.question: Two classes take the same test and have the same mean score. Class A has a standard deviation of \(2\), while Class B has a standard deviation of \(12\). What does this tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: Class B's scores are more spread out around the mean than Class A's scores

options.label: B
options.text: Class B's scores are more tightly clustered around the mean than Class A's scores

options.label: C
options.text: Both classes have identical distributions of scores

questions.explanation: Standard deviation, \(\sigma\), measures how spread out data values are from the mean. A larger standard deviation, like Class B's \(\sigma = 12\), means the scores are more widely spread compared to Class A's smaller \(\sigma = 2\), even though both classes share the same mean.
questions.hint: A larger standard deviation indicates greater variability, not a different average.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a data set.
questions.question: A set of test scores was recorded as \(22, 22, 8, 72\). What is the mean of this data set?
questions.explanation: Sum all the values: \(22 + 22 + 8 + 72 = 124\). Divide by the number of values, \(n=4\): \(\bar{x} = \frac{124}{4} = 31\).
questions.hint: Add all the values together, then divide by how many values there are: \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}\).

questions.learningObjective: Find a missing value in a data set given the mean and the other observations.
questions.question: A data set of \(5\) plant heights (cm) has a mean of \(46.2\). If \(4\) of the values are \(44, 50, 37, 58\), what is the missing value?
questions.explanation: Since the mean is \(46.2\) for \(n=5\) values, the total sum must be \(46.2 \times 5 = 231\). The known values sum to \(189\), so the missing value is \(231 - 189 = 42\).
questions.hint: Multiply the mean by the number of values to find the total sum, then subtract the known values.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a relative frequency as a percentage from a frequency table.
questions.question: A survey of 51 people asked their favorite color, with results: Red: 13; Blue: 11; Green: 13; Yellow: 14. What percentage of respondents chose Yellow, the most popular color? Round to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: The frequency for Yellow is \(14\) out of \(51\) total respondents. The percentage is \(\frac{14}{51} \times 100\% \approx 27.5\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the frequency of the category by the total number of respondents, then multiply by 100.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a claim about a data set is mathematically consistent with a given mean.
questions.question: A data set has \(n=5\) values with a mean of \(22\). A student claims that all 5 values in the data set are greater than \(27\). Is this possible?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because the sum of the values would then exceed the total implied by the mean

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, this is always possible regardless of the mean

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, as long as the median is also greater than the mean

questions.explanation: If the mean is \(22\) for \(n=5\) values, the total sum must be \(22 \times 5 = 110\). If every value were greater than \(27\), the sum would have to exceed \(135\), which is greater than \(110\). This is a contradiction, so it is impossible for all values to exceed the mean by that much.
questions.hint: Check whether the claim is consistent with the total sum implied by the mean: \(\text{sum} = \bar{x} \times n\).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the arithmetic mean of a data set.
questions.question: A set of test scores was recorded as \(81, 35, 64, 55\). What is the mean of this data set?
questions.explanation: Sum all the values: \(81 + 35 + 64 + 55 = 235\). Divide by the number of values, \(n=4\): \(\bar{x} = \frac{235}{4} = 58.75\).
questions.hint: Add all the values together, then divide by how many values there are: \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}\).

questions.learningObjective: Find a missing value in a data set given the mean and the other observations.
questions.question: A data set of \(5\) video views (thousands) has a mean of \(33.6\). If \(4\) of the values are \(28, 51, 30, 34\), what is the missing value?
questions.explanation: Since the mean is \(33.6\) for \(n=5\) values, the total sum must be \(33.6 \times 5 = 168\). The known values sum to \(143\), so the missing value is \(168 - 143 = 25\).
questions.hint: Multiply the mean by the number of values to find the total sum, then subtract the known values.
